title: What Do You Need Wednesday One Frame at a Time
author: Episcopal Academy Center for Teaching and Learning
summary: This installment of the Episcopal Academy Center for Teaching and Learning's weekly roundup curates three items with editorial commentary and a classroom 'Try This' for each, framed around the idea that early-year learning leaves traces only if teachers look for them. The first item summarizes a paper classifying student responses to peer feedback as acceptance, elaboration, modification, or no uptake, highlighting that offering a specific fix roughly tripled acceptance while naming an issue halved non-uptake. The second introduces Gemini Notebook's Expert Intelligence feature, which lets readers query an owned ebook such as David Epstein's Range alongside author-edited supplements. The third reports a classroom study with Italian fifth graders in which fill-in-the-gap testing with self-correction produced 67.7% accuracy versus 41.3% for rereading, while extending the spacing gap from one to four days added nothing. The issue closes with a time-lapse of starling murmurations as an image of patterns accumulating across ordinary school days. Learning & Curriculum is the dominant bucket because two of the three items are learning-science findings on feedback and retrieval; the AI tool item is secondary.
points: The peer feedback paper sorts revisions into acceptance, elaboration, modification, and no uptake, and CTL suggests students label their own revision decisions using those categories.
Specific suggested fixes roughly tripled acceptance of peer feedback, and clearly naming a perceived problem made students about half as likely to ignore it.
In a real-classroom history study, fill-in-the-gap retrieval with answer-key correction yielded 67.7% final accuracy against 41.3% for unlimited rereading.
Lengthening the interval between first reading and study from one to four days produced no spacing benefit (44.6% versus 45.9%), a result CTL flags as surprising.
The recommended routine is to open class with production from memory, then immediately provide correct versions and require every student to fix errors before moving on.
quotes: We are less than two weeks into the school year, and as a result almost nothing is visible yet. Students are forming habits you can’t see, and so are we.

Acceptance meant that a student applied the comment as given and changed little else. Elaboration saw students respond to the comment, but in doing so they frequently added more evidence or additional reasoning, which the reviewer never asked for.

And this is the part that likely matters most if you run peer review in your classroom: when students were offered a specific fix, that roughly tripled the acceptance response and clearly naming a perceived issue made no uptake about half as likely.

Expert Intelligence lets you load an ebook you own into a notebook as a queryable source—and David Epstein'sRange is one of the titles that launched with it, complete with supplemental materials Epstein reviewed and edited himself.

We are often cautious of sharing overt research findings from labs as being something teachers ought to immediately replicate in their classrooms. But when the research originates in real classrooms, consider our interest piqued.
Students either re-read a history text as many times as they wanted, or they took a fill-in-the-gap test on it. Testing produced 67.7% accuracy on the final assessment; re-reading produced 41.3%.

Interestingly, researchers also lengthened the gap between first reading and study session from one day to four, expecting spacing to add something. In reality it did not, with a success rate of 44.6% versus 45.9%.
Then, hand them the correct versions immediately. Don’t move on until each student has corrected their mistakes.
